faq_info: What is the Paris-Éducation website for?
faq_info_description: This website helps students and visitors discover Paris, its monuments, its history and its main attractions. It provides clear, educational and accessible information.
faq_localisation_description: Paris, the capital of France, is located in the north-central part of the country, in the heart of the Île-de-France region. The city is crossed by the Seine River and lies in the center of the Paris Basin.
faq_arriver_description: Choose your preferred mode of transport: plane for international flights or coach for budget connections to Paris. Follow the instructions below for arriving in the city.
faq_plan_3days: 3 days: Day 1 → Eiffel Tower + Notre-Dame (evening illuminations). Day 2 → Louvre Museum + Seine walk. Day 3 → Palace of Versailles.
faq_plan_4days: 4 days: Day 4 → Disneyland Paris (early morning + fireworks in the evening).
faq_conseil_description: Buy tickets online 2–3 weeks in advance to avoid queues and save time on site.

versailles_description:
The Palace of Versailles was built between 1623 and 1624 by Louis XIII as a hunting residence in a marshy area. This initial building, called the “small castle,” was medium-sized and mainly used for private stays. After a period of neglect, it was expanded by Louis XIV from 1664 through the 17th century, with the help of architects such as Louis Le Vau and Jules Hardouin-Mansart. The additions included new wings, the famous Hall of Mirrors, and extensive French-style gardens. 
 From 1682 to 1789, Versailles became the royal residence where the king, the court, and even the government lived, reflecting the absolute monarchy of the time. During the French Revolution, the Estates-General of 1789 were held here before the king moved back to Paris. 
 Since then, Versailles became a museum in 1796 and was turned into a Museum of French History in 1837 by Louis-Philippe. It also served as the seat of government from 1871 to 1879. After restoration in the 20th century, it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
visite_guidée_description: An official Château guide (available in French, English, Romanian upon reservation) lasts 1.5–2 hours. It presents: daily life of Louis XIV, secrets of the Hall of Mirrors, court intrigues, symbols of absolute power, and the history of Le Nôtre’s gardens. Price: around +€10.

disney_histoire:
Disneyland opened its doors on April 12, 1992 under the name Euro Disney and is the first themed destination in Europe inspired by the Disney worlds. Built in Marne-la-Vallée near Paris, Disneyland quickly faced financial difficulties due to high prices, lower-than-expected visitor numbers, and a vulnerable structure, leading to significant losses. 
 In 2002, a second park called Walt Disney Studios opened on March 16, 2002, turning the destination into a cinema and animation-themed complex. Expansions include attractions such as Ratatouille in 2014, the Avengers Campus in 2022, and several areas related to Star Wars, Snow White, and Marvel. A €2 billion expansion has doubled the size of the second park and added a lake, nighttime shows, and Frozen-themed areas.
d_1: Big Thunder Mountain – mine train roller coaster, 3 min duration, max speed 45 km/h, 35 m drop, 5 trains
d_2: Pirates of the Caribbean – boat dark ride, 10 min duration, immersive scenes from the Pirates of the Caribbean films
d_3: Star Wars Hyperspace Mountain – indoor roller coaster, 2:30 duration, 50 km/h, 1 loop, 32 m height
d_4: Avengers Assemble: Flight Force – launch roller coaster, up to 80 km/h, Marvel theme, inversions
d_5: Crush's Coaster – spinning roller coaster, 2 min duration, 45 km/h, 12 m height, wild rotation

louvre_histoire:
The Louvre began in 1190 under Philip II as a fortress to protect Paris and control the Seine. It included a keep, towers, and moats. In the 14th century, it was transformed into a royal residence by Charles V. From 1546, Francis I began transforming the Louvre into a Renaissance palace under the direction of Pierre Lescot, a process continued under Henry II. Henry IV connected the Louvre to the Tuileries via the Grande Galerie in 1594, marking the beginning of the complex’s expansion. Work continued under Louis XIII and Louis XIV, including the enlargement of the Cour Carrée and the Colonnade. 
 After Louis XIV moved to Versailles in 1678, the Louvre ceased to be a royal residence and instead became a place to store royal collections. The museum opened on August 10, 1793 during the French Revolution as the Central Museum of the Arts. It was later renamed the Musée Napoléon under Napoleon I. 
 In the 20th century, the Louvre was modernized, notably with the glass pyramid inaugurated in 1989 by I. M. Pei to attract tourists.
louvre_joconde: Painted by Leonardo da Vinci between 1503 and 1506 (and retouched until 1519) in Florence and later in France. It is the portrait of Lisa Gherardini (wife of a Florentine merchant). Technique: sfumato (soft blending of tones). Stolen in 1911, recovered in 1913.
louvre_milo: Hellenistic Greek sculpture (c. 150–100 BC), discovered in 1820 by a farmer on the island of Milos. Offered to Louis XVIII. Missing arms likely broke during transport or in battle.
louvre_victoire: Hellenistic statue (c. 190 BC) representing the goddess Nike. Discovered in 1863 by Charles Champoiseau on the island of Samothrace. Head and arms missing. Placed on the Daru staircase for dramatic effect.

histoire_nd:
The construction of Notre-Dame de Paris took place between 1163 and 1345. It began under Maurice de Sully, Bishop of Paris, to replace an older Romanesque church. Radiating chapels and sculpted elements, such as scenes from the life of Christ on the north wall, were added until the 14th century during the reign of Philip IV the Fair. 
 A major fire devastated the cathedral on April 15, 2019. It destroyed the roof, the spire, and much of the main structure, while damaging the organ and stained glass windows. Restoration efforts brought together international funding and a team of project leaders, including architects such as Philippe Villeneuve, to rebuild oak structures and restore stained glass and sculptures. 
 The cathedral reopened on December 7, 2024 during a ceremony attended by President Emmanuel Macron and Pope Francis. The restored spire, gargoyles, and stained glass windows were reinstated, allowing daily services to resume. The current rector, Olivier Ribadeau Dumas, appointed in September 2022, oversees liturgical activities.

tresor: Treasure – sacred relics including the Crown of Thorns (acquired by Saint Louis in 1239 in Constantinople for 135,000 livres)
couronne_epines: Crown of Thorns – kept in a crystal reliquary since the 2024 restoration
gargouilles: Gargoyles – 13th century, sculptures used to drain rainwater and protect against spirits (54 gargoyles + 28 chimeras)

restaurant2_nd: Café Saint-Régis – chic café on Île Saint-Louis with direct view of Notre-Dame
restaurant3_nd: Berthillon – legendary artisan ice cream on Île Saint-Louis (3 min away)

eiffel-histoire:
The Eiffel Tower was built by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Paris Universal Exhibition marking the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. The tower was initially criticized by prominent figures such as Alexandre Dumas and Émile Zola, who saw it as an eyesore. However, despite opposition, the project—based on engineering innovations from the United States and the United Kingdom—won the 1886 competition and was awarded a 6.5 million franc contract in 1887. 
 Built by 250 workers in two years (1887–1889) on the Champ de Mars, the Eiffel Tower was inaugurated on March 31, 1889. It was the tallest structure in France until 1930. From its early days, it served scientific purposes, including meteorology and radio transmission experiments. In 1898 and 1903, Gustave Ferrié conducted early wireless telegraphy experiments there, proving its strategic value during World War I. 
 Saved from demolition in 1909 due to its scientific importance, its concession was extended by 70 years in 1910. Major renovations took place in the 1980s to reduce weight and improve safety, and again between 2018 and 2022 in preparation for the 2024 Olympic Games, including temporary installation of Olympic rings.
eiffel_fact1: It was the tallest structure in the world until 1930
eiffel_fact2: Repainted every 7 years (3 tons of paint)
eiffel_fact3: It sways up to 15 cm in the wind
eiffel_fact5: Weighs 10,000 tons and survived planned demolition in 1940
eiffel_restaurant1: Le Jules Verne – Michelin-starred restaurant on the 1st floor of the Tower
eiffel_restaurant2: 58 Tour Eiffel – chic brasserie with panoramic views
eiffel_restaurant3: Café Constant (5 min away) – traditional French cuisine, great value
champ_mars: Champ de Mars – the large park right at the foot of the Tower. Ideal for picnics, photos, or relaxing after the visit (grass, fountains, stunning view).
eiffel_etape1: From central Paris, take line 6 toward Charles de Gaulle–Étoile or Nation.
eiffel_etape3: Use the “Eiffel Tower” exit and walk about 300 meters to the base of the tower.
eiffel_etape4: Alternative: take line 8 to École Militaire, then a 10-minute walk along Avenue de Suffren.
eiffel_info:
Address: 5 Avenue Anatole France, 75007 Paris
Hours: Daily 9:30–23:00
Top floor ticket (elevator): up to €36.70 (adult)
Highlights: Wrought iron structure, historic elevators, orientation tables, 20,000-bulb light show
advice-eiffel: To get the most out of the Eiffel Tower, book an early guided tour and combine it with priority access to the summit. This virtual visit already gives a good overview of the route and best viewpoints.
